floors.name: Vectors and the Space They Live In

sections.title: A Vector Is a List, and Also an Arrow
sections.body:
A **vector** in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an ordered list of $n$ real numbers, written $\mathbf{v} = (v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n)$; the numbers are its **components** and $n$ is fixed once and for all by the space you are working in. That is the whole definition - there is nothing hidden inside a vector beyond its list of components.

The second picture is geometric: $\mathbf{v}$ is the arrow from the origin to the point with those coordinates, so a vector carries a direction and a length without being pinned anywhere except the origin. The two readings are the same object, and the skill worth building on this floor is switching between them at will.

We work in $\mathbb{R}^n$ because it is the smallest setting in which everything later - matrices, projections, eigenvectors - already makes sense. You lose the picture beyond $n = 3$, but not one line of the algebra.

Order and length both matter: $(3,-1)$ and $(-1,3)$ are different vectors, and $(3,-1)$ is not $(3,-1,0)$, because those two do not even live in the same set.
sections.code:
A vector in R^n is an ordered list of n real numbers.

  v = (3, -1, 2)          a vector in R^3
      ^   ^   ^
      |   |   +-- third component,  v_3 = 2
      |   +------ second component, v_2 = -1
      +---------- first component,  v_1 = 3

Same object, drawn: an arrow from the origin (0,0,0) to the point (3,-1,2).

  R^1   the number line             v = (3)
  R^2   the plane                   v = (3, -1)
  R^3   ordinary space              v = (3, -1, 2)
  R^5   no picture, same algebra    v = (3, -1, 2, 0, 7)

ORDER MATTERS.  (3, -1) and (-1, 3) are different vectors: one points
right-and-down, the other left-and-up.

LENGTH MATTERS.  (3, -1) lives in R^2 and (3, -1, 0) lives in R^3.
They are not the same vector; they are not even in the same set.

annotations.text: The components are indexed from 1 and the order is part of the data. Swap two of them and you have a different vector.
The arrow starts at the origin. That is a convention, and it is what lets one arrow stand for one list of numbers with no ambiguity.
R^5 has no drawing, yet every rule on this floor still applies to it unchanged. This is why we define vectors by components rather than by pictures.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill each blank with a plain integer.
checkpoint.template:
A vector in R^7 has ___ components.
The vector (3, -1, 2) lives in R^___.
The second component of (4, 0, -6) is ___.
checkpoint.explain: The superscript in $\mathbb{R}^n$ counts components and nothing else, so a vector of $\mathbb{R}^7$ has exactly seven of them. The tempting slip on the last blank is to read off $-6$: components are numbered left to right starting at $1$, so the second component of $(4,0,-6)$ is the middle entry $0$.

sections.title: Two Operations, Done One Slot at a Time
sections.body:
Only two operations are defined on vectors, and both act componentwise: $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = (u_1+v_1, \dots, u_n+v_n)$ and $c\mathbf{v} = (cv_1, \dots, cv_n)$ for a real **scalar** $c$. Nothing couples the slots to each other, which is exactly why $\mathbb{R}^n$ is so easy to compute in.

Geometrically, addition is tip-to-tail: slide $\mathbf{v}$ until its tail meets the tip of $\mathbf{u}$, and $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ is the arrow closing the path. Equivalently it is the diagonal of the parallelogram spanned by the two arrows, which is the picture that makes $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}$ obvious.

Scalar multiplication stretches: $c > 1$ lengthens, $0 < c < 1$ shortens, a negative $c$ flips the arrow to the opposite side of the origin, and $c = 0$ collapses it to the origin. The direction survives scaling up to that flip, so $c\mathbf{v}$ never leaves the line through $\mathbf{v}$ and the origin.

Subtraction is not a third operation: $\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}$ means $\mathbf{u} + (-1)\mathbf{v}$. And a sum of vectors from different $\mathbb{R}^n$ is undefined rather than false, because there is no slot to pair the extra components with.
sections.code:
u = (3, -1, 2)      v = (-1, 4, 0)      both in R^3

Addition and scaling work one slot at a time, independently:

  u + v   = (3 + (-1),   -1 + 4,    2 + 0)    = (2, 3, 2)
  u - v   = (3 - (-1),   -1 - 4,    2 - 0)    = (4, -5, 2)
  2u      = (2*3,        2*(-1),    2*2)      = (6, -2, 4)
  -v      = (-1*(-1),    -1*4,      -1*0)     = (1, -4, 0)

  2u - 3v = (6, -2, 4) - (-3, 12, 0)          = (9, -14, 4)

What the two operations do to the arrows:

  u + v    slide v until its tail sits on the tip of u; the sum is the
           arrow from the tail of u to the new tip of v.  (Tip to tail.)
  2u       same direction, twice as long.
  -u       same line, opposite direction.
  0u       collapses to the origin, whatever u was.

Adding a vector of R^3 to a vector of R^2 is not wrong, it is undefined:
there is no third slot in the R^2 vector to add anything to.

annotations.text: Slot 1 never talks to slot 2. Every componentwise identity you will meet reduces to ordinary arithmetic repeated n times.
2u - 3v is a single linear combination with coefficients 2 and -3, evaluated by scaling first and adding second.
Scaling by 0 sends every vector to the same place, the origin. That collapse is where the zero vector comes from.

checkpoint.prompt: Let $\mathbf{a} = (4, 0, -2)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (1, -3, 5)$. Give each component as a plain integer.
checkpoint.explain: Every entry is one line of ordinary arithmetic: $-2 + 5 = 3$ in the third slot of the sum, and $-2 - 5 = -7$ in the third slot of the difference. The usual error is dropping a sign when subtracting a negative component, so read $\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}$ as $\mathbf{a} + (-1)\mathbf{b}$ and the signs take care of themselves.

sections.title: The Eight Rules, and What They Buy
sections.body:
The two operations obey eight rules: addition commutes and associates, there is a **zero vector** $\mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v}$, every $\mathbf{v}$ has an additive inverse $-\mathbf{v}$, $1\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}$, $c(d\mathbf{v}) = (cd)\mathbf{v}$, and multiplication distributes both over vector sums and over scalar sums. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ each of them is just the corresponding rule for real numbers applied in every slot at once.

They earn their keep because any set obeying all eight is called a **vector space**, and everything proved from the eight alone transfers instantly to polynomials, matrices and functions. The axioms are the interface; $\mathbb{R}^n$ is only the first implementation of it.

The zero vector is worth naming carefully. It is the vector all of whose components are $0$, it is unique, and it is the one point every span, every line through the origin and every plane through the origin must contain.

A small but genuine theorem: $0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for every $\mathbf{v}$. It is not an axiom and it is not a definition - it is forced, and the worked example derives it from the rules.
sections.code:
The eight rules.  u, v, w are vectors in R^n; c, d are real numbers.

  1  u + v = v + u                    addition commutes
  2  (u + v) + w = u + (v + w)        addition associates
  3  v + 0 = v                        a zero vector exists
  4  v + (-v) = 0                     every vector has an inverse
  5  1 v = v                          the scalar 1 does nothing
  6  c(d v) = (cd) v                  scalars associate
  7  c(u + v) = cu + cv               distributes over a vector sum
  8  (c + d) v = cv + dv              distributes over a scalar sum

They are not decoration.  Rules 3, 4 and 8 alone force  0v = 0:

  0v = (0 + 0)v            since 0 = 0 + 0 in the reals
     = 0v + 0v             rule 8
  now add -(0v) to both sides:
  0v + (-(0v)) = (0v + 0v) + (-(0v))
  0            = 0v + 0                 rules 2 and 4
  0            = 0v                     rule 3

So the zero vector is not merely "the arrow of no length" by decree.  It is
the unique vector that leaves every vector unchanged under addition, and it
is where every scaling by the number 0 is forced to land.

annotations.text: Rules 3 and 4 assert existence. They are what make 0 and -v available at all, rather than being facts about particular components.
The trick is rewriting the scalar 0 as 0 + 0 so that rule 8 has something to distribute over. Nothing about components is used.
Cancelling by adding an inverse is the only cancellation available: there is no division of vectors anywhere in this subject.

checkpoint.prompt: The identity $0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ looks like a definition, yet it is proved. Explain why it must be a theorem rather than an axiom, and name the two rules that do the real work in the derivation.
checkpoint.explain: The eight axioms never mention the number $0$ multiplying a vector, so the value of $0\mathbf{v}$ is not stipulated anywhere - it is squeezed out by rewriting $0$ as $0+0$ and letting the distributive rule for scalar sums turn $0\mathbf{v}$ into $0\mathbf{v} + 0\mathbf{v}$. Adding the additive inverse of $0\mathbf{v}$ then cancels one copy and leaves $\mathbf{0}$. Assuming it as an axiom would be harmless but redundant, and it would hide the fact that the result holds in every vector space, not only in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

sections.title: Linear Combinations and the Shape of a Span
sections.body:
A **linear combination** of $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k$ is any vector $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k$ with real coefficients $c_i$. It is the only kind of expression the two operations can build, so it is the central construction of the whole subject.

The **span** of a list of vectors is the set of every linear combination of them: $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k\} = \{c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k : c_i \in \mathbb{R}\}$. Asking whether $\mathbf{w}$ lies in a span is therefore always the same question: does a system of equations in the coefficients have a solution?

Geometrically the span of one non-zero vector is the line through the origin along it, and the span of two vectors pointing in different directions is the plane through the origin containing both. If the second vector is a multiple of the first it adds no new direction, and the span stays a line.

Two facts hold no matter what: every span contains $\mathbf{0}$, taking all coefficients zero, and $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{0}\}$ is the single point $\{\mathbf{0}\}$. A span is never a line or a plane that misses the origin.
sections.code:
A linear combination of v1, ..., vk is any vector

  c1 v1 + c2 v2 + ... + ck vk         with c1, ..., ck real numbers.

The span is the set of ALL of them:  span{v1, ..., vk}.

ONE VECTOR.  span{(2,1)} = { t(2,1) : t real }, the line through the origin
and the point (2,1).  Unless v = 0: span{(0,0)} = {(0,0)}, a single point.

TWO VECTORS, different directions.  span{(1,2),(3,-1)} is all of R^2.
Test it on (9,4).  Solve  a(1,2) + b(3,-1) = (9,4):

       a + 3b = 9
      2a -  b = 4      =>   b = 2a - 4,  a + 6a - 12 = 9,  a = 3, b = 2

  check:  3(1,2) + 2(3,-1) = (3,6) + (6,-2) = (9,4).            yes

TWO VECTORS, same direction.  span{(1,2),(2,4)} is still only the line
through (1,2), because (2,4) = 2(1,2) contributes no new direction.

IN R^3.  span{(1,1,0),(0,1,1)} = { (a, a+b, b) } = the plane x - y + z = 0.
  (3,5,2):  a = 3, b = 2, and a + b = 5.   3 - 5 + 2 = 0.       in span
  (7,7,7):  a = 7, b = 7 force a + b = 14, not 7.  7 - 7 + 7 = 7.   not in

Every span contains the zero vector: take every coefficient to be 0.

annotations.text: The parameter t sweeps out the whole line as it runs over the reals, negative values covering the half on the far side of the origin.
Membership of a span has become a 2x2 system of linear equations. Every later method in this dungeon is a better way of solving exactly this.
Two vectors in R^3 sweep out a plane, never all of R^3: two coefficients cannot reach three independent directions.

checkpoint.prompt: Write $(1, 11)$ as a linear combination of $(2,1)$ and $(-1,3)$. Set up the system in the two unknown coefficients, solve it, and verify your answer by substitution.
checkpoint.explain: Matching components gives $2c_1 - c_2 = 1$ and $c_1 + 3c_2 = 11$, whose solution is $c_1 = 2$, $c_2 = 3$; substituting back, $2(2,1) + 3(-1,3) = (4,2) + (-3,9) = (1,11)$. The point of the exercise is not the arithmetic but the translation: a question about membership of a span turned, with no cleverness at all, into a system of linear equations.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the vocabulary. The first three blanks take one word each; the last takes a plain integer.
guided-practice.template:
The individual numbers making up a vector are its ___.
A plain real number multiplying a vector is called a ___.
The vector whose every component is 0 is the ___ vector.
The number of components of a vector in R^4 is ___.
guided-practice.explain: The words matter because the two operations treat scalars and vectors as different kinds of thing: a scalar rescales, a vector translates, and the two are never added to one another. Calling the entries components rather than coordinates also keeps the list reading and the arrow reading of a vector deliberately separate.

guided-practice.prompt: Let $\mathbf{p} = (2, -3)$ and $\mathbf{q} = (-1, 5)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Give each component as a plain integer.
guided-practice.explain: For the last line, scale before you subtract: $2\mathbf{q} = (-2, 10)$, so $\mathbf{p} - 2\mathbf{q} = (2 - (-2), -3 - 10) = (4, -13)$. The classic wrong answers $(0,-13)$ and $(4,7)$ come from subtracting $\mathbf{q}$ once and doubling afterwards, or from letting the minus sign reach only one component.

guided-practice.prompt: Let $\mathbf{u} = (3,-1,2)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (-1,4,0)$. Evaluate each expression, writing every answer in the form `(a, b, c)` with plain integers.
guided-practice.explain: Each line is one linear combination $c_1\mathbf{u} + c_2\mathbf{v}$ evaluated slot by slot: for the third, $2(3,-1,2) = (6,-2,4)$ and $3(-1,4,0) = (-3,12,0)$, and subtracting gives $(9,-14,4)$. The last line is the geometry of the floor in miniature - scaling by $0$ destroys all information about $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, which is why every span, whatever it is built from, contains the origin.

guided-practice.prompt: Express $(8,3)$ as a linear combination of $(1,3)$ and $(2,-1)$. Write down the two equations that come from matching components, solve for both coefficients, and verify the result by substituting back.
guided-practice.explain: Matching the first components gives $a + 2b = 8$ and the second gives $3a - b = 3$; eliminating $b$ yields $7a = 14$, so $a = 2$ and $b = 3$, and indeed $2(1,3) + 3(2,-1) = (2,6) + (6,-3) = (8,3)$. Matching components is legal precisely because equality of vectors means equality in every slot - two vectors are equal when their lists are, not when they merely look alike.

guided-practice.prompt: Describe the geometry of $\mathrm{span}\{(2,1)\}$, of $\mathrm{span}\{(2,1),(1,3)\}$ and of $\mathrm{span}\{(2,1),(4,2)\}$, all inside $\mathbb{R}^2$. Say what each set is as a picture, and explain why the third differs from the second.
guided-practice.explain: One non-zero vector spans the line through the origin along it, so $\mathrm{span}\{(2,1)\}$ is that line and nothing more. Adding $(1,3)$, which points in a genuinely different direction, lets the two coefficients reach every point of the plane, so the span is all of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Adding $(4,2)$ instead adds nothing, because $(4,2) = 2(2,1)$ already lies on the first line - the count of vectors is never what matters, only the count of distinct directions.

problem-set.prompt: Let $\mathbf{u} = (1,1,0)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (0,1,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Decide whether $(3,5,2)$ lies in $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\}$ and whether $(7,7,7)$ does. In each case set up the system in the two coefficients and say exactly which equation succeeds or fails.
problem-set.answer: (3,5,2) is in the span with a = 3, b = 2; (7,7,7) is not
problem-set.explain: Writing $a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{v} = (a, a+b, b)$ makes both questions mechanical: the outer components fix $a$ and $b$ immediately, and the middle component is the only real test. For $(3,5,2)$ we get $a = 3$, $b = 2$ and $a + b = 5$, which holds, so the vector is in the span. For $(7,7,7)$ we get $a = 7$, $b = 7$, forcing $a + b = 14 \neq 7$, so the system is inconsistent and no combination whatsoever produces it.

problem-set.prompt: Consider $\mathbf{a} = (2,-1,3)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (-4,2,-6)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Describe $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\}$ geometrically, justifying your description. Then decide, with reasons, whether $(6,-3,9)$ and $(2,-1,4)$ belong to it.
problem-set.answer: a line through the origin; (6,-3,9) is in it, (2,-1,4) is not
problem-set.explain: Since $\mathbf{b} = -2\mathbf{a}$, every combination $c_1\mathbf{a} + c_2\mathbf{b} = (c_1 - 2c_2)\mathbf{a}$ collapses to a single multiple of $\mathbf{a}$, so the span is the line through the origin along $\mathbf{a}$ rather than a plane. Then $(6,-3,9) = 3\mathbf{a}$ is on that line, while $(2,-1,4)$ is not: matching the first two components demands the multiplier $1$, which would give a third component of $3$, not $4$. The trap is counting vectors instead of directions - two listed vectors do not guarantee a two-dimensional span.

problem-set.prompt: Let $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $S = \mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\}$. Prove that if $\mathbf{w}_1, \mathbf{w}_2 \in S$ and $k$ is any real number, then $\mathbf{w}_1 + \mathbf{w}_2 \in S$ and $k\mathbf{w}_1 \in S$. Name the axioms you use, and say why the argument never inspects a single component.
problem-set.explain: Write the two arbitrary members as $\mathbf{w}_1 = a_1\mathbf{u} + b_1\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}_2 = a_2\mathbf{u} + b_2\mathbf{v}$; commutativity and associativity of addition regroup the sum, and distributivity over scalar sums collects it as $(a_1+a_2)\mathbf{u} + (b_1+b_2)\mathbf{v}$, which is again a linear combination. Similarly $k\mathbf{w}_1 = (ka_1)\mathbf{u} + (kb_1)\mathbf{v}$, using distributivity over a vector sum and associativity of scalars. No component is ever touched, which is exactly why the same proof shows spans are closed in any vector space and not only in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

problem-set.prompt: Prove that $0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for every $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n$, using only the eight axioms and never the components of $\mathbf{v}$. Then use the result to explain why every span, of any list of vectors whatsoever, must contain the zero vector.
problem-set.answer: 0v = 0, so taking every coefficient to be 0 puts the zero vector in every span
problem-set.explain: The derivation rewrites the scalar as $0 = 0 + 0$, applies distributivity over a scalar sum to get $0\mathbf{v} = 0\mathbf{v} + 0\mathbf{v}$, then adds the additive inverse of $0\mathbf{v}$ to both sides to cancel one copy and leave $\mathbf{0}$. The consequence is geometric: choosing every coefficient to be $0$ in a linear combination produces $0\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + 0\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}$, so no span can avoid the origin. That is why a span is always a line or plane *through* the origin and never a shifted one.

problem-set.prompt: A student writes $(1,2) + (1,2,0) = (2,4,0)$, reasoning that the missing third component of the first vector must be $0$. Explain precisely why the sum is undefined rather than merely unconventional, and what it would cost to make it legal.
problem-set.explain: Addition is defined only between two vectors of the same $\mathbb{R}^n$, because it is defined slot by slot and there is no slot in $(1,2)$ to pair with the third component of $(1,2,0)$ - the two vectors are elements of different sets. To make the expression legal you must first choose an embedding of $\mathbb{R}^2$ into $\mathbb{R}^3$, appending a $0$, and that is an extra map you supplied rather than something the definition hands you. The student's answer is what you get after that choice, which is why the reasoning feels harmless and is nevertheless an unstated assumption.

exam.prompt: A **linear combination** of the vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k$ is:
choices: any vector $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k$ with real coefficients $c_1, \dots, c_k$
any vector of the form $\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + \mathbf{v}_k$, with no coefficients allowed
any vector $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k$ whose coefficients are all non-zero
the list $(c_1, \dots, c_k)$ of coefficients used to build such a vector
exam.explain: The coefficients range over all real numbers, zero and negative ones included, which is what makes the set of combinations closed and what puts $\mathbf{0}$ inside every span. The third choice describes a strictly smaller collection and would break that closure, while the last confuses the combination, which is a vector, with the recipe that built it.

exam.prompt: For vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the **span** is:
choices: the number of vectors in the list
the set of all linear combinations of $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k$
the smallest line containing all of $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k$
the set $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k\}$ itself
exam.explain: A span is a set of vectors, not a count and not the original list, and it is generally far larger than the list it is built from. The third choice fails as soon as two of the vectors point in different directions, since no line can then contain them all - the span may be a point, a line, a plane or the whole space.

exam.prompt: Complete the four axioms. Each blank takes a single symbol: `u`, `v` or `0`.
exam.template:
For all u, v:  u + v = v + ___
There is a vector 0 with v + 0 = ___ for every v.
Every v has an inverse -v with v + (-v) = ___.
For every v, the scalar 1 satisfies 1 v = ___.
exam.explain: The middle two lines are the axioms asserting that something *exists* - a zero vector, and an inverse for each vector - rather than stating an equality between things already in hand. The rule $1\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}$ looks too trivial to state, but without it nothing forbids a scaling operation that sends every vector to the origin, and the eight rules would no longer pin down what a vector space is.

exam.prompt: Let $\mathbf{c} = (1,-2,4)$ and $\mathbf{d} = (3,0,-1)$. Give each component as a plain integer.
exam.explain: The third line is the one worth checking twice: $3\mathbf{c} = (3,-6,12)$ and $2\mathbf{d} = (6,0,-2)$, and adding gives $(9,-6,10)$. Scaling must happen before adding, since $3(\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{d}) = (12,-6,9)$ is a different vector entirely - a coefficient belongs to one vector, never to the sum.

exam.prompt: Arrange these lines into a correct solution showing that $(9,4)$ lies in $\mathrm{span}\{(1,2),(3,-1)\}$.
fragments: Seek real numbers $a, b$ with $a(1,2) + b(3,-1) = (9,4)$.
Matching components gives the system $a + 3b = 9$ and $2a - b = 4$.
The second equation gives $b = 2a - 4$; substitute it into the first.
Then $a + 3(2a-4) = 9$, so $7a = 21$ and $a = 3$, hence $b = 2$.
exam.explain: The order encodes the method: name the unknown coefficients, turn vector equality into a system by matching components, solve the system, and only then verify. Jumping straight to a system without declaring what $a$ and $b$ are leaves the equations meaning nothing, and the closing substitution is what converts a solved system back into an answer about membership of the span.

exam.prompt: Let $\mathbf{a} = (4,0,-2)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (1,-3,5)$. Evaluate each expression, writing every answer in the form `(a, b, c)` with plain integers.
exam.explain: The middle two steps pull on the same pair in different ways: subtraction flips $\mathbf{b}$ before adding, giving $-2 - 5 = -7$ in the last slot, while scaling touches only $\mathbf{a}$. The final step combines the axiom $1\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a}$ with the theorem $0\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$, and it is the reason each generating vector always sits inside the span it helps to generate.

exam.prompt: Let $S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1)\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Show that a vector $(x,y,z)$ lies in $S$ exactly when $x - y + z = 0$, and use that test to decide the membership of $(2,5,3)$ and of $(1,0,2)$.
exam.explain: A general element is $a(1,1,0) + b(0,1,1) = (a, a+b, b)$, so $x = a$ and $z = b$ are forced and the only condition left is $y = a + b = x + z$, which rearranges to $x - y + z = 0$. Testing, $2 - 5 + 3 = 0$ so $(2,5,3) \in S$ with $a = 2$, $b = 3$, while $1 - 0 + 2 = 3 \neq 0$ so $(1,0,2) \notin S$. Turning a span into a single equation is the first glimpse of a theme running through this whole dungeon: a subspace can be described either by what generates it or by what it satisfies.

exam.prompt:
Justify each step of this derivation by naming the axiom or result it uses:
$$\mathbf{v} + (-1)\mathbf{v} = 1\mathbf{v} + (-1)\mathbf{v} = (1 + (-1))\mathbf{v} = 0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}.$$
Then state what the derivation proves about $(-1)\mathbf{v}$, and why that is a result rather than a definition.
exam.answer: 1v = v, distributivity over scalar sums, arithmetic, then 0v = 0; hence (-1)v is the additive inverse of v
exam.explain: The first step is the identity axiom $1\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}$ read backwards, the second is distributivity over a sum of scalars, the third is arithmetic in $\mathbb{R}$, and the last is the theorem $0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. The conclusion is that $(-1)\mathbf{v}$ satisfies the defining property of an additive inverse, so $(-1)\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}$ - the axioms promise only that *some* inverse exists, and this identifies it as scaling by $-1$ instead of assuming it.

exam.prompt: Explain why no span can be a line that misses the origin, and why $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{0}\}$ is a single point rather than the empty set. Then say what geometric object $\mathrm{span}\{(2,1),(4,2)\}$ is, and why.
exam.explain: Setting every coefficient to $0$ is always a legal choice, so $\mathbf{0}$ belongs to every span without exception and a line avoiding the origin cannot be one. For the same reason $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{0}\}$ contains $\mathbf{0}$ and nothing else, making it the single point at the origin rather than empty. And since $(4,2) = 2(2,1)$ contributes no new direction, $\mathrm{span}\{(2,1),(4,2)\}$ is only the line through the origin along $(2,1)$ - a reminder that a shifted line, the natural home of an inhomogeneous solution set, is never a span.

floors.name: Systems, and the Matrix That Holds Them

lesson.title: Systems, and the Matrix That Holds Them

sections.title: One Equation Instead of Many
sections.body:
A linear system is usually written as a list of equations, but the list is a poor object to reason about: it has no shape. Collect the coefficients into a matrix $A$, the unknowns into a column $\mathbf{x}$ and the right-hand sides into a column $\mathbf{b}$, and the whole list becomes the single statement $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$.

Read that statement **one row at a time** and you get the row picture: each equation is a line in the plane, a plane in space, a hyperplane in general, and a solution is a point lying on all of them at once.

Read it **one column at a time** and you get the column picture, which is the more useful of the two: $A\mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{a}_1 + x_2\mathbf{a}_2 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{a}_n$, a weighted combination of the columns of $A$. Solving then asks a single question - *which recipe of the columns produces $\mathbf{b}$?* - and the three possible answers (exactly one recipe, no recipe, endlessly many recipes) are already visible as geometry before any arithmetic starts.
sections.code:
System of two equations:      2x -  y = 1
                               x +  y = 5

As one matrix equation  A x = b :

    [ 2  -1 ] [ x ]   [ 1 ]
    [ 1   1 ] [ y ] = [ 5 ]
      A          x      b

ROW picture - read A x = b one row at a time.
    Each equation is a line in the plane.
    The two lines meet at exactly one point: (x, y) = (2, 3).
    Check:  2(2) - (3) = 1     (2) + (3) = 5

COLUMN picture - read A x = b one column at a time.
    A x is a combination of the columns of A, weighted by x and y:

        x * [ 2 ]  +  y * [ -1 ]  =  [ 1 ]
            [ 1 ]         [  1 ]     [ 5 ]

    The right weights are x = 2, y = 3:

        2 * [ 2 ]  +  3 * [ -1 ]  =  [ 4 - 3 ]  =  [ 1 ]
            [ 1 ]         [  1 ]     [ 2 + 3 ]     [ 5 ]

annotations.text: The unknowns sit in a column, not a row. That is what makes A x a legal product: A has two columns and x has two rows.
Two lines in the plane either cross once, are parallel and never cross, or are the same line. Those are exactly the three outcomes this floor is about.
This is the definition of A x that matters: the entries of x are the weights on the columns of A.

checkpoint.prompt: The system $3x + 5y = 7$, $\;x - 2y = 4$ is written as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$. Fill in the missing entries of $A$ and $\mathbf{b}$. Type numbers only, with a minus sign where needed.
checkpoint.explain: The rows of $A$ follow the equations in order and each column belongs to one unknown, so the second column collects the $y$ coefficients $5$ and $-2$. The sign travels with the coefficient: writing $2$ instead of $-2$ silently solves $x + 2y = 4$, a different system with a different answer.

sections.title: The Augmented Matrix and Its Three Legal Moves
sections.body:
Once a system is $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, the symbols $x$, $y$, $z$ are pure decoration - they only mark which column a number sits in. Strip them out and glue $\mathbf{b}$ on as one more column and you have the **augmented matrix** $[\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$, which carries every scrap of information the system had and nothing else.

Only three moves are ever performed on it, the **elementary row operations**: swap two rows, multiply a row by a non-zero constant, or add a multiple of one row to a different row.

Each of the three is chosen because it is **reversible** by another operation of the same kind - and that is the whole reason they may be trusted. If $\mathbf{x}$ satisfies the old rows it satisfies the new ones, and because the move can be undone, the converse holds too, so the two systems have exactly the same solution set and are called **equivalent**.

The insistence that $c \neq 0$ in the scaling rule is not fussiness: multiplying a row by $0$ throws an equation away and can only enlarge the solution set.
sections.code:
System                          Augmented matrix  [ A | b ]

  x + 2y +  z =  2                 [ 1  2  1 |  2 ]
 3x + 8y +  z = 12                 [ 3  8  1 | 12 ]
      4y +  z =  2                 [ 0  4  1 |  2 ]

Note the 0 in the bottom-left cell: the third equation has no x term,
so its x coefficient is zero and the cell must be filled in.

The three elementary row operations, and the undo of each:

  1. SWAP     Ri <-> Rj                        undo: swap them back
  2. SCALE    Ri <- c * Ri,  c not zero        undo: Ri <- (1/c) * Ri
  3. REPLACE  Ri <- Ri - k * Rj,  i not j      undo: Ri <- Ri + k * Rj

Because every operation has an undo of the same kind, any (x, y, z)
satisfying the old rows satisfies the new ones and vice versa. The
matrix changes; the solution set does not.

annotations.text: Missing variables are not missing entries. Every column of the augmented matrix must be filled, with 0 where a variable does not appear.
Scaling by c = 0 has no undo - 1/0 does not exist - which is exactly why the definition forbids it.
Ri <- Ri - k*Rj changes only row i. Row j is untouched, and that is what keeps the move reversible.

checkpoint.prompt: Name each elementary row operation. Each blank takes exactly one lower-case word: swap, multiply or add.
checkpoint.template:
___ two rows.
___ a row by a non-zero constant.
___ a multiple of one row to a different row.
checkpoint.explain: There are exactly three because exactly three reversible moves are needed: reordering equations, rescaling one, and combining two. A fourth tempting move - adding a multiple of a row to *itself* - is not on the list, since $R_i \leftarrow R_i - 1\cdot R_i$ would destroy the row and could not be undone.

sections.title: Gaussian Elimination, Start to Finish
sections.body:
**Gaussian elimination** is the disciplined use of the third row operation to manufacture zeros. Work left to right: take the first non-zero entry of the top row as the **pivot**, use it to clear every entry below it in that column, then move down and right to the next pivot and repeat.

When no more can be cleared, the matrix is in **row echelon form**: every pivot lies strictly to the right of the pivot above it, and any all-zero rows have sunk to the bottom. The system now looks triangular, and the bottom equation involves one unknown, so it can be solved and pushed upwards - this is **back substitution**.

Pressing on - scaling each pivot to $1$ and clearing *above* it as well - gives the **reduced row echelon form**, which is unique for a given matrix and needs no back substitution at all: the answer is simply sitting in the last column. That extra work is Gauss-Jordan elimination.

Elimination is not a trick for small systems; it is the algorithm, costing roughly $n^3/3$ multiplications on an $n \times n$ system, and every serious solver is a refinement of it.
sections.code:
Solve   x + 2y +  z =  2
       3x + 8y +  z = 12
            4y +  z =  2

FORWARD ELIMINATION

  [ 1  2  1 |  2 ]
  [ 3  8  1 | 12 ]     R2 <- R2 - 3 R1
  [ 0  4  1 |  2 ]

  [ 1  2  1 |   2 ]
  [ 0  2 -2 |   6 ]    R3 <- R3 - 2 R2
  [ 0  4  1 |   2 ]

  [ 1  2  1 |   2 ]    <- row echelon form U
  [ 0  2 -2 |   6 ]       pivots 1, 2, 5 sitting in columns 1, 2, 3
  [ 0  0  5 | -10 ]

BACK SUBSTITUTION, bottom row upwards

  5z = -10                 ->  z = -2
  2y - 2z = 6  -> 2y + 4 = 6  ->  y = 1
  x + 2y + z = 2 -> x + 2 - 2 = 2 ->  x = 2

GAUSS-JORDAN: keep going to reduced row echelon form

  [ 1  0  0 |  2 ]
  [ 0  1  0 |  1 ]     the solution is read straight off
  [ 0  0  1 | -2 ]

Check:  1(2) + 2(1) + (-2) = 2      3(2) + 8(1) + (-2) = 12
                            4(1) + (-2) = 2

annotations.text: The pivot is the 1 in the top-left. R2 - 3 R1 is chosen precisely so the 3 beneath it becomes 0.
Row echelon form: pivots 1, 2 and 5 step to the right as you go down. That staircase is what 'echelon' means.
Back substitution runs upwards, so each equation has exactly one unknown left by the time you reach it.
In reduced row echelon form each pivot is 1 and is the only non-zero entry in its column, so the last column IS the solution.

checkpoint.prompt: Take one elimination step on $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 9 & 11 \end{bmatrix}$, using row 1 to clear the $2$. State the operation you used and the resulting second row.
checkpoint.answer: R2 <- R2 - 2 R1, giving the new row 2 = [0 1 5]
checkpoint.explain: The multiplier is the entry to be killed divided by the pivot, here $2/1 = 2$, which is why the operation is $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ and the new row is $[\,0\;\;1\;\;5\,]$. Adding rather than subtracting is the usual slip and yields $[\,4\;\;17\;\;17\,]$, which clears nothing.

sections.title: Unique, None, or Infinitely Many
sections.body:
A linear system has exactly three possible fates, and echelon form names which one before any answer is written down. Columns carrying a pivot correspond to **pivot variables**; columns with no pivot correspond to **free variables**, which may be set to anything.

If some row of the echelon form reads $[\,0\;0\;\cdots\;0 \mid c\,]$ with $c \neq 0$, that row asserts $0 = c$ and the system is **inconsistent**: no solution at all. Geometrically the columns of $A$ simply cannot combine to reach $\mathbf{b}$.

Otherwise the system is consistent, and the count decides. Every unknown a pivot variable means a **unique** solution; one or more free variables means **infinitely many**, one for each choice of the free values, and the solution set is a line, a plane or a higher flat rather than a point.

Notice what this rules out: a linear system can never have exactly two or exactly seventeen solutions. If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ both solve it, so does every point on the line joining them, so two solutions force infinitely many.
sections.code:
Same coefficients, two different right-hand sides.

  x + 2y -  z = 3            x + 2y -  z = 3
 2x + 5y +  z = 8           2x + 5y +  z = 8
 3x + 7y      = 10          3x + 7y      = 11

  [ 1  2 -1 |  3 ]           [ 1  2 -1 |  3 ]
  [ 2  5  1 |  8 ]           [ 2  5  1 |  8 ]
  [ 3  7  0 | 10 ]           [ 3  7  0 | 11 ]

R2 <- R2 - 2R1,  R3 <- R3 - 3R1,  then R3 <- R3 - R2 :

  [ 1  2 -1 |  3 ]           [ 1  2 -1 |  3 ]
  [ 0  1  3 |  2 ]           [ 0  1  3 |  2 ]
  [ 0  0  0 | -1 ]           [ 0  0  0 |  0 ]

  last row says 0 = -1       last row says 0 = 0
  NO SOLUTION                2 pivots, 3 unknowns -> z is free

                             back-substituting with z = t:
                               y = 2 - 3t
                               x = 3 - 2y + z = -1 + 7t
                             INFINITELY MANY: (-1+7t, 2-3t, t)

A third case: if elimination had produced a pivot in every one of the
three unknown columns and no 0 = c row, the solution would be UNIQUE.

annotations.text: Only the last entry of the third equation differs: 10 on the left, 11 on the right. The coefficient matrix is identical.
0 = -1 is false for every (x, y, z), so no vector can satisfy the system. Nothing about the coefficients caused this - b did.
0 = 0 is true and simply says the third equation carried no new information; it was the sum of the other two in disguise.
t is the free variable. Each value of t gives a different genuine solution, so the solution set is a line in space.

checkpoint.prompt: After elimination an augmented matrix has 4 unknowns, 3 pivots and no row of the form $[\,0\;0\;0\;0 \mid c\,]$ with $c \neq 0$. How many solutions does the system have, and why?
checkpoint.explain: No $0 = c$ row means the system is consistent, and $4$ unknowns against $3$ pivots leaves exactly one free variable, so the solution set is a line and there are infinitely many solutions. The tempting answer 'none, because there are fewer pivots than unknowns' confuses a shortage of pivots, which creates freedom, with an inconsistent row, which destroys solutions.

guided-practice.prompt: Write the augmented matrix of the system below. Fill in the missing second row. Type numbers only, using a minus sign where the coefficient is negative.
guided-practice.explain: The second equation has no $y$ term, and 'no $y$ term' means the coefficient is $0$, not that the entry is skipped - every column must be filled or the columns stop lining up with the unknowns. The leading $x$ with no written coefficient is $1$, another entry that is easy to leave blank.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the definitions. Each blank takes exactly one lower-case word: pivot, free, echelon or reduced.
guided-practice.template:
The first non-zero entry of a row, once elimination has finished, is called a ___ .
A matrix whose pivots step strictly rightwards as you go down is in row ___ form.
A column of the coefficient matrix carrying no pivot belongs to a ___ variable.
If in addition every pivot is 1 and is alone in its column, the matrix is in ___ row echelon form.
guided-practice.explain: Echelon form asks only for the descending staircase of pivots; reduced form adds two further demands, that each pivot equals $1$ and that its column is otherwise empty. Confusing the two is why learners stop eliminating too early and then wonder why the answer is not readable in the last column.

guided-practice.prompt: Put these steps into the order Gaussian elimination performs them when solving a $3 \times 3$ system by hand.
fragments: Write the system as the augmented matrix $[\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$.
Take the first non-zero entry of row 1 as the pivot of column 1.
Clear the entries below that pivot with $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - m_{21}R_1$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - m_{31}R_1$.
Move to column 2 and use the new pivot in row 2 to clear the entry below it.
Read the bottom equation, which now has one unknown, and solve it.
Back-substitute that value upwards to recover the remaining unknowns.
guided-practice.explain: Elimination is strictly downward and left to right: column 2 is only touched once column 1 is finished, because clearing column 1 changes rows 2 and 3 and would undo any earlier work on them. Back substitution then runs the other way, upwards, which is why it can only begin after the whole forward sweep is complete.

guided-practice.prompt: Forward-eliminate $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & 9 & -3 & 8 \\ -2 & -3 & 7 & 10 \end{bmatrix}$ using the operations named below, in that order. After each one, give the row that changed as four numbers separated by single spaces, for example: 0 1 1 4
guided-practice.explain: The multiplier for row 2 is $4/2 = 2$ and for row 3 is $-2/2 = -1$, so row 3 is *added* rather than subtracted - the sign of the multiplier follows the entry being killed. Each operation uses the current row 3, not the original one, which is why the last step starts from $[\,0\;\;1\;\;5\;\;12\,]$ and not from $[-2\;\;{-3}\;\;7\;\;10]$.

guided-practice.prompt: The augmented matrix $[\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$ drops the letters $x$, $y$, $z$ and the equals signs entirely. Explain what information it still carries and what has genuinely been discarded.
guided-practice.explain: Nothing mathematical is lost: each coefficient is still present and its column records which unknown it multiplies, so position replaces naming. What is discarded is only the labels themselves - the matrix cannot tell you whether column two was called $y$ or $q$, which is exactly why the columns must be kept in a fixed order and zeros written for absent terms.

elimination-drills.prompt:
Solve by Gaussian elimination, showing the augmented matrix at each stage:
$$\begin{aligned} x + y + z &= 4 \\ x + 2y + 3z &= 9 \\ 2x + 3y + z &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
elimination-drills.explain: With $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - R_1$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 2R_1$ the first column clears to give rows $[\,0\;1\;2\mid 5\,]$ and $[\,0\;1\;-1 \mid -4\,]$; then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_2$ leaves $-3z = -9$, so $z = 3$, $y = 5 - 2(3) = -1$ and $x = 4 - (-1) - 3 = 2$. Three pivots for three unknowns is what guarantees the answer is unique; substituting back into all three original equations is the only check worth trusting.

elimination-drills.prompt: Reduce the augmented matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 2 & 6 & 3 & 7 & 14 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 5 & 9 \end{bmatrix}$ (four unknowns $x_1,\dots,x_4$) to **reduced** row echelon form. State which columns hold pivots, which variables are free, and give the general solution.
elimination-drills.answer: RREF rows [1 3 0 -1 | 1], [0 0 1 3 | 4], [0 0 0 0 | 0]; pivots in columns 1 and 3; x2 and x4 free; x1 = 1 - 3x2 + x4, x3 = 4 - 3x4
elimination-drills.explain: $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_1$ both produce $[\,0\;0\;1\;3\mid 4\,]$, so the third row cancels to zero and the pivots land in columns 1 and 3 only; clearing above the second pivot with $R_1 \leftarrow R_1 - R_2$ finishes the reduction. Column 2 never receives a pivot because it is three times column 1, and a pivotless column is precisely a free variable - counting pivots by counting rows rather than by locating them is the standard error here.

elimination-drills.prompt: Eliminate on $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 & 8 \\ 3 & 7 & 0 & 10 \end{bmatrix}$ and say what the resulting echelon form tells you about the solution set. Justify your conclusion from the echelon form itself, not by guessing.
elimination-drills.answer: Echelon form has final row [0 0 0 | -1], asserting 0 = -1, so the system is inconsistent and has no solution.
elimination-drills.explain: $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 3R_1$ give identical left-hand parts $[\,0\;1\;3\,]$ but right-hand sides $2$ and $1$, so $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_2$ produces $[\,0\;0\;0 \mid -1\,]$ - the equation $0 = -1$, which no vector satisfies. The trap is reading the row of zeros on the left as 'a free variable, so infinitely many'; the deciding entry is the one after the bar, and $-1 \neq 0$ makes the system inconsistent instead.

elimination-drills.prompt: Elimination has produced the row echelon form $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 & -9 \end{bmatrix}$ for unknowns $x, y, z$. Carry out back substitution, giving each value as a plain number such as -2.
elimination-drills.explain: The bottom row is the only one with a single unknown, which is why substitution must start there: $-3z = -9$ gives $z = 3$, then $y + 2(3) = 5$ gives $y = -1$, then $x + (-1) + 3 = 4$ gives $x = 2$. Working top-down instead leaves three unknowns in the first equation and gets nowhere - echelon form is useful precisely because it is triangular from the bottom.

elimination-drills.prompt: A single row operation turned $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 7 & 16 \end{bmatrix}$ into $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Identify the operation exactly, state the operation that undoes it, and explain why the two augmented matrices describe systems with the same solution set.
elimination-drills.answer: R2 <- R2 - 3 R1; the undo is R2 <- R2 + 3 R1; both systems have solution x = 3, y = 1
elimination-drills.explain: The multiplier is read off the entry that vanished, $3/1 = 3$, and the whole row must move together - $16 - 3(5) = 1$ confirms it. Because $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 + 3R_1$ restores the original exactly, any solution of one system is a solution of the other, and both give $x = 3$, $y = 1$; an irreversible move such as multiplying a row by $0$ would break that argument in one direction only.

solution-analysis.prompt: Why is a system obtained by elementary row operations guaranteed to have exactly the same solution set as the original - not merely a solution set that contains it? Argue from the operations themselves.
solution-analysis.explain: Every operation is easily seen to send solutions forwards - a vector satisfying two equations satisfies any combination of them - but that argument alone only proves containment one way. The second inclusion comes from reversibility: each of the three operations is undone by another of the same kind, so the same forwards argument applied to the undo carries solutions back, and the two sets are equal. Scaling by $0$ is barred for exactly this reason, since it has no undo and can strictly enlarge the solution set.

solution-analysis.prompt: Let $S$ be the system with rows $E_1, E_2, \dots, E_m$ and let $S'$ be identical except that $E_2$ is replaced by $E_2 - kE_1$. Prove that $S$ and $S'$ have the same solution set.
solution-analysis.explain: The proof is two inclusions. If $\mathbf{v}$ satisfies $S$ then it satisfies $E_1$ and $E_2$, hence the combination $E_2 - kE_1$, and every other row is untouched, so $\mathbf{v}$ satisfies $S'$. Conversely, if $\mathbf{v}$ satisfies $S'$ it satisfies $E_1$ and $E_2 - kE_1$, so it satisfies $(E_2 - kE_1) + kE_1 = E_2$ - and it is the availability of that undo, not any special property of $k$, that supplies the converse. Proving only the first direction is the usual gap, and it would leave open the possibility that $S'$ had gained solutions.

solution-analysis.prompt:
The systems below share a coefficient matrix and differ only in the last entry of $\mathbf{b}$. Classify each outcome and give the full solution set of whichever one is consistent.
$$\begin{aligned} x + 2y - z &= 3 & x + 2y - z &= 3 \\ 2x + 5y + z &= 8 & 2x + 5y + z &= 8 \\ 3x + 7y &= 10 & 3x + 7y &= 11 \end{aligned}$$
solution-analysis.answer: Left: no solution. Right: infinitely many, (x, y, z) = (-1 + 7t, 2 - 3t, t) for every real t.
solution-analysis.explain: Both eliminate to the same left-hand echelon form with pivots in columns 1 and 2 and a zero third row; the only difference is the final entry, $-1$ on the left and $0$ on the right. So the left system contains $0 = -1$ and is inconsistent, while the right one is consistent with $z$ free, giving $y = 2 - 3t$ and $x = 3 - 2y + z = -1 + 7t$. The lesson is that consistency is a property of $\mathbf{b}$ relative to the columns of $A$, not of $A$ alone - identical coefficients decided nothing here.

solution-analysis.prompt: Give the running time of Gaussian elimination on a dense $n \times n$ system, as a function of $n$, and justify it by counting the work the algorithm actually does.
solution-analysis.explain: Clearing below the first pivot touches about $n$ rows of about $n$ entries each, costing $n^2$; the next pivot works on an $(n-1) \times (n-1)$ block, and so on, and $n^2 + (n-1)^2 + \cdots$ is roughly $n^3/3$, which is cubic. Back substitution is only $O(n^2)$ and so is invisible in the total - a common wrong answer is $O(n^2)$, obtained by counting the entries of the matrix once instead of counting how many times each is rewritten.

exam.prompt: A matrix is in **reduced row echelon form** exactly when:
choices: it is in row echelon form, every pivot equals $1$, and each pivot is the only non-zero entry in its column
it is square and every entry below the main diagonal is zero
it is in row echelon form and has no rows of zeros
every entry is either $0$ or $1$
exam.explain: Reduced form adds two requirements to echelon form - pivots normalised to $1$ and their columns cleared above as well as below - and it is these that let the solution be read straight from the last column. The second choice describes an upper-triangular matrix, which need not have its pivots ordered or normalised, and zero rows are perfectly legal in reduced form, where they signal a dependent equation.

exam.prompt: Which of the following are **elementary row operations**? Select every one that is.
choices: Interchange rows $2$ and $4$
Replace $R_3$ by $5R_3$
Replace $R_3$ by $0 \cdot R_3$
Replace $R_2$ by $R_2 - 4R_1$
Interchange columns $1$ and $3$
exam.explain: The three legal moves are swapping rows, scaling a row by a **non-zero** constant, and adding a multiple of one row to a different row; each is reversible, which is what protects the solution set. Scaling by $0$ has no undo and simply deletes an equation, while swapping columns is not a row operation at all - it reorders the unknowns and would leave the answer permuted.

exam.prompt: The augmented matrix of a system in unknowns $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4$ has reduced row echelon form $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 4 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$. Fill in the blanks with a number, a number, and the name of the free variable written like x3.
exam.template:
Number of pivots: ___
Number of free variables: ___
The free variable is ___
exam.explain: Pivots sit in columns $1$, $2$ and $4$ of the coefficient part, so three unknowns are determined and the pivotless column $3$ gives the single free variable $x_3$. Counting the last column as a fourth pivot is the classic slip: that column holds $\mathbf{b}$, and a pivot there would mean $0 = c$ and no solutions at all.

exam.prompt: Arrange these into the order Gauss-Jordan elimination performs them when producing reduced row echelon form.
fragments: Form the augmented matrix $[\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]$.
Sweep forwards, clearing all entries below each pivot in turn, to reach row echelon form.
Scale each pivot row so that every pivot equals $1$.
Sweep backwards, clearing the entries above each pivot.
Read the values of the pivot variables from the final column.
exam.explain: The upward sweep can only begin once the pivots are known, and the pivots are only known when the forward sweep has finished, so the order of the two sweeps is forced. Reading the last column first is the mistake worth naming: before the columns above the pivots are cleared, the last column still holds partially eliminated constants, not the solution.

exam.prompt: Forward-eliminate $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 & 8 \\ 3 & 7 & 0 & 11 \end{bmatrix}$ with the operations named below, in order. Give each changed row as four numbers separated by single spaces.
exam.explain: Rows 2 and 3 reduce to the identical row $[\,0\;1\;3\mid 2\,]$, which is what makes the third step annihilate the row completely: the third equation was the sum of the first two and carried no new information. A row of zeros right across, bar included, is harmless - it costs a pivot and creates a free variable rather than destroying the solution set.

exam.prompt: During elimination a row becomes $[\,0\;\;0\;\;0 \mid 7\,]$. State precisely what this says about the original system, and contrast it with a row that becomes $[\,0\;\;0\;\;0 \mid 0\,]$.
exam.explain: $[\,0\;0\;0 \mid 7\,]$ is the equation $0 = 7$, false for every vector, so the original system - being equivalent to this one - is inconsistent and has no solution whatever the other rows say. $[\,0\;0\;0\mid 0\,]$ is the harmless statement $0 = 0$: the row was redundant, the system loses a pivot, and the usual consequence is a free variable and infinitely many solutions.

exam.prompt:
Solve completely, by elimination on the augmented matrix:
$$\begin{aligned} x + 3y + 2z &= 5 \\ 2x + 7y + 7z &= 9 \\ 2x + 5y + 2z &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
exam.explain: $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 2R_1$ give $[\,0\;1\;3\mid -1\,]$ and $[\,0\;-1\;-2\mid 0\,]$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 + R_2$ leaves $z = -1$, whence $y = -1 - 3(-1) = 2$ and $x = 5 - 3(2) - 2(-1) = 1$. Three pivots in three unknown columns and no $0 = c$ row is exactly the signature of a unique solution, so no free variable and no parameter should appear in the answer.

exam.prompt: A system of $3$ equations in $4$ unknowns is eliminated and no row of the form $[\,0\;0\;0\;0 \mid c\,]$ with $c \neq 0$ appears. Show that it cannot have exactly one solution, and say what its possible outcomes are.
exam.answer: At least one column has no pivot, so there is at least one free variable and the system has infinitely many solutions.
exam.explain: Each pivot occupies its own row, so three rows admit at most three pivots among four unknown columns, leaving at least one pivotless column - a free variable. The absence of a $0 = c$ row makes the system consistent, and a consistent system with a free variable has one solution for every value of that variable, hence infinitely many; the only outcomes available to a wide system are therefore none or infinitely many, never exactly one.

sections.title: The Only Combination That Vanishes
sections.body:
A list of vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$ is **linearly independent** when the equation $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution $c_1 = \dots = c_k = 0$. Everything hangs on the word *only*: the trivial solution is always available, so the definition is really asking whether the zero vector can be reached in a second, less obvious way.

If it can, the list is **linearly dependent**, and the offending coefficient list is a **dependence relation**. Solve that relation for any vector carrying a non-zero coefficient and you have written that vector in terms of the others, which is the geometric content: a dependent list repeats a direction it already had.

Dependence is a property of the whole list, not of its pairs. Three vectors can be pairwise non-parallel and still dependent, because the redundancy only surfaces when all three are combined - $\mathbf{u}_3$ may sit in the plane spanned by $\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\mathbf{u}_2$ without being a multiple of either.

Two consequences come for free: any list containing $\mathbf{0}$ is dependent, since $1 \cdot \mathbf{0}$ vanishes on its own, and any list with a repeated vector is dependent too.
sections.code:
Independence, stated once:

  c1*v1 + c2*v2 + ... + ck*vk = 0   forces   c1 = c2 = ... = ck = 0

The zero vector is always reachable by taking every ci = 0.  That is the
TRIVIAL combination and it costs nothing.  The real question is whether any
OTHER combination also lands on 0.

  v1 = (1, 2, 3)      v2 = (2, 4, 6)

  2*v1 + (-1)*v2 = (2-2, 4-4, 6-6) = (0, 0, 0)

  A non-trivial combination reaches 0, so {v1, v2} is DEPENDENT.
  Geometrically v2 lies on the line through v1: it adds no new direction.

  u1 = (1, 0, 1)      u2 = (0, 1, 1)      u3 = (1, 1, 2)

  1*u1 + 1*u2 + (-1)*u3 = (0, 0, 0)

  Non-trivial again, so {u1, u2, u3} is DEPENDENT - and here no single
  vector is a scalar multiple of any other.  Dependence is a statement
  about the WHOLE set, never about one pair inside it.

annotations.text: Read this as an implication, not as an equation to solve. Independence claims the vanishing combinations are exhausted by the boring one.
The coefficients (2, -1) are the dependence relation. Rearranged they say v2 = 2*v1, which is what redundancy looks like in coordinates.
Pairwise independence is strictly weaker than independence. Here u3 = u1 + u2 lies in the plane of the first two without being parallel to either.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the definition and the worked dependence. The first two blanks take one word each; the third takes an integer.
checkpoint.template:
If the only solution of c1*v1 + ... + ck*vk = 0 is c1 = ... = ck = 0, that solution is the ___ one and the list is linearly ___.
For v1 = (1,2,3) and v2 = (2,4,6), a vanishing combination is 2*v1 + ___*v2 = 0.
checkpoint.explain: The trivial solution is free of charge for any list whatsoever, so it can never distinguish one list from another; independence is the claim that nothing else works. Here $\mathbf{v}_2 = 2\mathbf{v}_1$, so $2\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{0}$ is a genuine non-trivial relation and the pair is dependent.

sections.title: Testing Independence by Elimination
sections.body:
The definition is a statement about a homogeneous system, so elimination decides it outright. Stack $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$ as the **columns** of a matrix $A$; then $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k = A\mathbf{c}$, and the list is independent exactly when $A\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$ forces $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$.

Row operations rewrite the rows of $A$ but never disturb the solution set of $A\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$, so reduce $A$ to echelon form and count pivots. Every pivot column corresponds to a coefficient elimination pins down; every **free** column corresponds to a coefficient you may set to $1$, manufacturing a non-zero solution by back-substitution.

The test is therefore a count: the list is independent if and only if every column is a pivot column, that is $\operatorname{rank} A = k$. When a free column exists the reduced form hands you the dependence relation explicitly, rather than merely announcing that one exists.

And because a matrix with $n$ rows admits at most $n$ pivots, any $k > n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are automatically dependent - there are not enough rows to go round.
sections.code:
Are the columns of A independent?  Solve A x = 0 and look.

        [ 1  2  1 ]
  A =   [ 2  4  3 ]
        [ 3  6  5 ]

  R2 <- R2 - 2*R1
  R3 <- R3 - 3*R1
        [ 1  2  1 ]
        [ 0  0  1 ]
        [ 0  0  2 ]

  R3 <- R3 - 2*R2
        [ 1  2  1 ]
        [ 0  0  1 ]
        [ 0  0  0 ]

  Pivots sit in columns 1 and 3.  Column 2 is FREE.
  A free column means A x = 0 has a non-zero solution,
  so the three columns are DEPENDENT.

  Reduced row echelon form:
        [ 1  2  0 ]
        [ 0  0  1 ]
        [ 0  0  0 ]

  The free column reads off x = (-2, 1, 0), that is
  (-2)*(col 1) + 1*(col 2) + 0*(col 3) = 0.

  Rule: independent  <=>  every column is a pivot column
                     <=>  rank = number of vectors.

annotations.text: Row operations are reversible, so they preserve the null space exactly. That is the licence for testing the original list on a reduced matrix.
Column 2 is free because no pivot lands in it. Setting its coefficient to 1 and back-solving produces a non-zero c, which is precisely a dependence.
Independence is thus a rank condition, and rank is something elimination computes. No guessing at combinations is ever required.

checkpoint.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 6 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$, answer each step. Give integers, or one word for the last step.

steps.label: Row 2 after R2 <- R2 - 2*R1, as three integers separated by spaces
Number of pivot columns of A
Number of free columns of A
Are the columns independent or dependent? One word.

checkpoint.explain: Subtracting $2R_1$ from $R_2$ clears the leading $2$ and also the $4$, because column 2 is exactly twice column 1, leaving $(0,0,1)$. Two pivots against three columns leaves one free column, and a free column is the signature of a non-zero solution of $A\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$ - so the count settles dependence before any relation is written down.

sections.title: A Basis Is Independent and Spanning
sections.body:
A **basis** of a vector space $V$ is a list that is linearly independent **and** spans $V$. The two conditions pull in opposite directions: spanning wants the list large enough to reach everything, independence wants it small enough to carry nothing redundant, and a basis is exactly the balance point.

Drop either half and the object stops doing its job. $\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0)\}$ is independent but misses most of $\mathbb{R}^3$; $\{(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^2$ but carries a passenger. Only a basis reaches every vector, and reaches it in exactly one way.

The **dimension** of $V$ is the number of vectors in a basis of $V$ - and that is a legitimate definition only because the number cannot depend on which basis you happened to pick. The proof is the pivot count from the previous section: $n$ vectors can never express $m > n$ independent ones, since the coefficient matrix would have a free column and hence a dependence.

So if two bases have $m$ and $n$ vectors, the argument run both ways gives $m \le n$ and $n \le m$, forcing $m = n$. Dimension is therefore an invariant of the space itself, and $\dim \mathbb{R}^n = n$ because the standard basis has $n$ members.
sections.code:
A BASIS of a vector space V is a list that is
   (1) linearly independent - nothing in it is redundant, and
   (2) spanning             - every v in V is some combination of it.

Independence alone is not enough:   {(1,0,0), (0,1,0)}  in R^3
   independent, but nothing in its span reaches (0,0,1).  Too small.

Spanning alone is not enough:       {(1,0), (0,1), (1,1)}  in R^2
   spans, but (1,1) = (1,0) + (0,1) is redundant.  Too big.

Three candidate lists in R^3, each tested by elimination:

  list                                 rank   size   verdict
  ----------------------------------------------------------
  {(1,0,2), (0,1,3), (1,1,6)}            3      3    BASIS
  {(1,2,-1), (2,1,3), (0,3,-5)}          2      3    dependent
  {(1,0,0), (0,1,0)}                     2      2    independent but
                                                     not spanning

WHY DIMENSION IS WELL DEFINED
  Suppose one basis has m vectors and another has n.  Each basis can be
  written in terms of the other, and elimination forbids n vectors from
  expressing m > n independent ones - the coefficient matrix would have
  a free column and hence a dependence.  So m <= n, and by symmetry
  n <= m, giving m = n.  That common number is dim V.  For R^n it is n.

annotations.text: An independent list that is too short spans only a subspace. It is a basis of that subspace, but not of the space you started in.
Rank 3 with 3 vectors in R^3 buys both halves at once: full rank means independent, and 3 pivots across 3 rows means the span is all of R^3.
Well-definedness is not a formality. Without it, 'the dimension' would be a property of a chosen list rather than of the space.

checkpoint.prompt: Decide whether $\{(1,0,2),(0,1,3),(1,1,6)\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$. Place the vectors in a matrix, reduce it, and justify **both** basis conditions from what the reduction tells you. State the rank and the dimension of the span.
checkpoint.answer: Yes - it is a basis of R^3; rank 3, span has dimension 3
checkpoint.explain: The reduction ends at the identity matrix, so all three columns are pivot columns: rank $3$ with $3$ vectors is independence. The same three pivots occupy all three rows, so $A\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{b}$ is solvable for every $\mathbf{b}$, which is spanning. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ a square full-rank matrix delivers both halves together, which is why $n$ independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ never need a separate spanning check.

sections.title: Coordinates and the Standard Basis
sections.body:
Once $B = (\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_n)$ is a basis of $V$, spanning says every $\mathbf{v}$ has an expansion $\mathbf{v} = c_1\mathbf{b}_1 + \dots + c_n\mathbf{b}_n$, and independence says the $c_i$ are **unique**. Subtract two expansions of the same $\mathbf{v}$ and the difference is a vanishing combination, which independence forces to be trivial - so the two expansions were one expansion all along.

That uniqueness is what makes the **coordinate vector** $[\mathbf{v}]_B = (c_1,\dots,c_n)$ well defined. A basis is thus a dictionary translating abstract vectors into lists of $n$ numbers, and finding coordinates is nothing more exotic than solving the linear system whose columns are the basis vectors.

The **standard basis** of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $E = (\mathbf{e}_1,\dots,\mathbf{e}_n)$, where $\mathbf{e}_i$ carries a $1$ in slot $i$ and $0$ elsewhere. It is independent because the combination $c_1\mathbf{e}_1 + \dots + c_n\mathbf{e}_n$ simply *is* the tuple $(c_1,\dots,c_n)$, so it vanishes only when every $c_i$ does, and spanning for the same reason.

The same observation gives $[\mathbf{v}]_E = \mathbf{v}$: the entries you have been writing all along were already coordinates, in the one basis whose coordinate map is the identity. Change the basis and the same arrow in space acquires a different list of numbers.
sections.code:
A basis turns vectors into lists of numbers.

If B = (b1, ..., bn) is a basis of V, every v in V is
   v = c1*b1 + ... + cn*bn
and the ci are UNIQUE.  Uniqueness IS independence:
   subtract two expansions of the same v and you get a
   vanishing combination, which independence forces to be trivial.

Write [v]_B = (c1, ..., cn), the COORDINATE VECTOR of v in B.

Example in R^2.   B = ( (1,1), (1,-1) ),   v = (3,5).

  a*(1,1) + b*(1,-1) = (3,5)
     a + b = 3
     a - b = 5      =>   a = 4,  b = -1

  Check: 4*(1,1) + (-1)*(1,-1) = (4-1, 4+1) = (3,5).   [v]_B = (4, -1)

THE STANDARD BASIS of R^n is E = (e1, ..., en), where ei carries a 1 in
slot i and 0 everywhere else.

  (7, -2, 5) = 7*e1 + (-2)*e2 + 5*e3        so  [(7,-2,5)]_E = (7, -2, 5)

The entries you have always written ARE coordinates - in E.  Nothing is
special about E beyond the fact that its coordinate map is the identity.

annotations.text: This is the load-bearing sentence of the section. Without independence a vector would have many coordinate vectors and the notation would name nothing.
Finding coordinates is solving a linear system whose coefficient matrix has the basis vectors as its columns. No new machinery is needed.
It is easy to mistake the standard basis for something canonical about vectors themselves. It is only the basis in which the translation step is invisible.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill in the two coordinate vectors as plain integers. $B = ((1,0,0),(1,1,0),(1,1,1))$ and $E$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
checkpoint.explain: Back-substitution gives $c_3 = 4$, then $c_2 + c_3 = 3$ so $c_2 = -1$, then $c_1 + c_2 + c_3 = 2$ so $c_1 = -1$; the check is $-1(1,0,0) - 1(1,1,0) + 4(1,1,1) = (2,3,4)$. The second line needs no work at all, and that is the point: in $E$ the coordinate map is the identity, so the habit of reading a tuple's entries as 'the' coordinates is correct in that one basis only.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the four core definitions. Each blank takes exactly one word.
guided-practice.template:
A list is linearly ___ when the only vanishing combination of it is the trivial one.
A list is linearly ___ when some combination with a non-zero coefficient equals the zero vector.
A ___ of V is a list that is both independent and spanning.
The number of vectors in any basis of V is the ___ of V.
guided-practice.explain: The four words form one chain: independence rules out redundancy, dependence names its failure, a basis adds spanning so nothing is missing either, and dimension is the count a basis certifies. Note the order of dependence between the ideas - dimension is defined through a basis and not the other way round, which is exactly why the well-definedness argument has to be made.

guided-practice.prompt: Put these steps into the correct order for testing whether $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are linearly independent.
fragments: Place the $k$ vectors as the columns of a matrix $A$, so that $c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k = A\mathbf{c}$.
Row reduce $A$ to echelon form, which alters the rows but leaves the solution set of $A\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$ untouched.
Mark the pivot columns and count them; that count is $\operatorname{rank} A$.
If all $k$ columns are pivot columns, the only solution is $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$ and the list is independent.
If some column is free, set its coefficient to $1$ and back-solve to read off an explicit dependence relation.
guided-practice.explain: Placing the vectors in the columns rather than the rows is the step most often inverted, and inverting it tests a different system entirely. Reduction must precede counting because pivots are a feature of echelon form, and the last two fragments are the two exits from the same count - a full set of pivots proves independence, a free column constructs the counterexample.

guided-practice.prompt: Let $A$ have columns $(1,-1,2)$, $(3,0,1)$ and $(1,2,-3)$, so $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$. Carry out the elimination and answer each step. Rows are three integers separated by spaces.

steps.label: Number of pivot columns of A

guided-practice.explain: After the two clearing operations rows 2 and 3 are $(0,3,3)$ and $(0,-5,-5)$, which are proportional, so the third row dies and only two pivots survive. Three vectors of rank $2$ leave one free column; back-solving gives $2\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{0}$, which you can check entrywise. The tempting error is to declare independence because no vector is visibly a multiple of another - a test that is simply not the definition.

guided-practice.prompt: Show that $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1,2,3)$, $\mathbf{v}_2 = (4,5,6)$ and $\mathbf{v}_3 = (7,8,9)$ are linearly dependent, and give an explicit dependence relation with integer coefficients. Obtain it by elimination rather than by inspection, and say which column of the reduced matrix produced it.
guided-practice.explain: The reduced form is $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, so column 3 is free; setting $c_3 = 1$ gives $c_1 = 1$ and $c_2 = -2$, that is $\mathbf{v}_1 - 2\mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{0}$. Entrywise, $1 - 8 + 7 = 0$, $2 - 10 + 8 = 0$ and $3 - 12 + 9 = 0$. Any non-zero multiple of those coefficients works equally well, because the dependence relations form a subspace rather than a single answer.

guided-practice.prompt: Explain why the dimension of a vector space is **well defined** - that is, why two different bases of the same space must contain the same number of vectors. Build the argument on the pivot count from elimination rather than quoting a theorem by name.
guided-practice.explain: Take bases of sizes $m$ and $n$. Every vector of the first is a combination of the second, so expressing all $m$ of them uses an $n \times m$ coefficient matrix; if $m > n$ that matrix has more columns than rows, hence a free column, hence a dependence among vectors that were assumed independent. So $m \le n$, and the symmetric argument gives $n \le m$. Without this, 'dimension' would describe a chosen list rather than the space, and calling $\mathbb{R}^3$ three-dimensional would be an accident of bookkeeping.

guided-practice.prompt: Let $B = ((2,1),(1,3))$. First confirm $B$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$, then compute $[\mathbf{v}]_B$ for $\mathbf{v} = (5,5)$. State the system you solved and say why its solution is unique.
guided-practice.explain: Neither column is a multiple of the other, so the $2 \times 2$ matrix has rank $2$ and $B$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Solving $2a + b = 5$ with $a + 3b = 5$ gives $a = 2$ and $b = 1$, and the check is $2(2,1) + 1(1,3) = (5,5)$. Uniqueness is not a lucky extra but the independence half of 'basis' wearing different clothes: a second expansion would subtract to a non-trivial vanishing combination.

problem-set.prompt: Determine whether $\{(1,2,-1),(2,1,3),(0,3,-5)\}$ is linearly independent in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Reduce the matrix whose columns are these vectors, report the rank and the number of free columns, and if the list is dependent write down an explicit relation with integer coefficients.
problem-set.explain: Reduction gives $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$: rank $2$, one free column, therefore dependent. Setting the free coefficient to $1$ yields $\mathbf{c} = (-2,1,1)$, and $-2(1,2,-1) + (2,1,3) + (0,3,-5) = (0,0,0)$ entrywise. Rank $2$ also reports the geometry - the three vectors lie in one plane through the origin, so their span is two-dimensional rather than all of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

problem-set.prompt: Prove both statements directly from the definition. (a) Any list of vectors containing the zero vector is linearly dependent. (b) Any list of $k$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $k > n$ is linearly dependent. For (b) argue through pivots, and say exactly which step uses the hypothesis $k > n$.
problem-set.explain: For (a) put the coefficient $1$ on the zero vector and $0$ on everything else: the combination equals $\mathbf{0}$ while the coefficient list is not all zero, so it is a dependence obtained with no computation. For (b) the matrix is $n \times k$; each pivot claims a distinct row, so there are at most $n$ pivots, and $k > n$ forces at least one column to be free - that is the sole use of the hypothesis. A free column yields a non-zero solution of $A\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$, so no list longer than $n$ is ever independent in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

problem-set.prompt: Let $B = (\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_n)$ span $V$. Prove that $B$ is linearly independent **if and only if** every $\mathbf{v} \in V$ has exactly one expansion $\mathbf{v} = c_1\mathbf{b}_1 + \dots + c_n\mathbf{b}_n$. Prove both directions, and in the harder direction say what you subtract and why the result is a vanishing combination.
problem-set.explain: Forwards: given two expansions of the same $\mathbf{v}$, subtract to obtain $\sum_i (c_i - d_i)\mathbf{b}_i = \mathbf{0}$; independence makes every $c_i - d_i$ zero, so the expansions coincide. Backwards: apply uniqueness to $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, which already owns the all-zeros expansion, so no other vanishing combination can exist - and that is independence. The equivalence is why coordinate vectors are legitimate notation at all: without independence $[\mathbf{v}]_B$ would name several different lists at once.

problem-set.prompt: Let $B = ((1,1,0),(0,1,1),(1,0,1))$. Prove that $B$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ by giving the rank of the matrix with these columns and drawing both basis conditions from it. Then compute $[(2,4,6)]_B$ and verify your answer by expanding it.
problem-set.explain: The matrix reduces to the identity, so rank is $3$: three pivots across three columns is independence, and three pivots across three rows makes $A\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{b}$ solvable for every $\mathbf{b}$, which is spanning. Solving $A\mathbf{c} = (2,4,6)$ gives $\mathbf{c} = (0,4,2)$, and indeed $0(1,1,0) + 4(0,1,1) + 2(1,0,1) = (2,4,6)$. A zero coordinate is not a warning sign - it merely says this vector needs none of that basis direction.

problem-set.prompt: Prove that the standard basis $E = (\mathbf{e}_1,\mathbf{e}_2,\mathbf{e}_3)$ really is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$, arguing from the definition rather than from a rank computation. Then state $[(7,-2,5)]_E$ and explain why the coordinate map in $E$ is the identity while in a general basis it is not.
problem-set.explain: The combination $c_1\mathbf{e}_1 + c_2\mathbf{e}_2 + c_3\mathbf{e}_3$ literally equals the tuple $(c_1,c_2,c_3)$, so the list spans - every tuple is reached by choosing its own entries - and it vanishes only when each $c_i = 0$, which is independence. Hence $[(7,-2,5)]_E = (7,-2,5)$. What is special is not the vectors but the bookkeeping: in $E$ the translation step is invisible, whereas in $B = ((1,1,0),(0,1,1),(1,0,1))$ the same arrow $(2,4,6)$ carries the quite different list $(0,4,2)$.

exam.prompt: The vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$ are **linearly independent** exactly when:
choices: no $\mathbf{v}_i$ is a scalar multiple of any other $\mathbf{v}_j$
$c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}$ has only the solution $c_1 = \dots = c_k = 0$
$c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}$ has no solution at all
the vectors together span the whole of $\mathbb{R}^k$
exam.explain: The third choice is impossible for any list whatsoever, since $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$ always solves a homogeneous system - which is precisely why the definition says *only* and not *no*. The first choice is pairwise independence, strictly weaker: $(1,0,1),(0,1,1),(1,1,2)$ satisfies it yet is dependent. The last confuses independence with spanning, the other half of a basis.

exam.prompt: A **basis** of a vector space $V$ is a list of vectors that is:
choices: spanning, and as large as possible
linearly independent and spanning
linearly independent, of size $\dim V$, and mutually orthogonal
any collection of $\dim V$ vectors drawn from $V$
exam.explain: Orthogonality is a later refinement and no part of the definition - $((1,1,0),(0,1,1),(1,0,1))$ is a perfectly good basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ containing no right angles. The last choice fails because the count alone is not enough: $\{(1,0),(2,0)\}$ has two members in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and spans only a line. The first inverts the balance, since a basis is as *small* as a spanning list can be.

exam.prompt: Fill in each blank. Three take an integer and one takes a single word.
exam.template:
dim(R^7) = ___
The largest possible size of a linearly independent list in R^4 is ___
Any 5 vectors in R^4 must be linearly ___
The standard basis of R^3 has ___ vectors.
exam.explain: All four answers descend from one fact: a matrix with $n$ rows admits at most $n$ pivots. That caps an independent list in $\mathbb{R}^4$ at four vectors and forces any five to be dependent, and since $\mathbf{e}_1,\dots,\mathbf{e}_n$ attains the cap while spanning, the dimension of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is exactly $n$.

exam.prompt: Arrange these lines into a valid proof that if $B = (\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_n)$ is independent then each $\mathbf{v}$ in its span has only one expansion in $B$.
fragments: Suppose $\mathbf{v} = c_1\mathbf{b}_1 + \dots + c_n\mathbf{b}_n$ and also $\mathbf{v} = d_1\mathbf{b}_1 + \dots + d_n\mathbf{b}_n$.
Subtract the second equation from the first, so the left-hand side becomes $\mathbf{0}$.
Collecting terms gives $(c_1-d_1)\mathbf{b}_1 + \dots + (c_n-d_n)\mathbf{b}_n = \mathbf{0}$, a vanishing combination of $B$.
